title: Financial Literacy and Personal Finance Management
subtitle: Measure your financial position, master interest and credit, protect what you build and follow a written personal financial plan.
description: A practical course in personal financial management for women in Nigeria and across Africa. You build your own net worth and cash flow statements, learn the arithmetic behind interest, inflation and loans, use credit and insurance wisely, secure your financial independence and finish with a Personal Financial Management Plan and a 90-day action path.
outcomes: Prepare a personal balance sheet and a monthly cash flow statement from real records
Score your financial health with five indicators and choose one priority
Calculate simple and compound interest, the yearly cost of monthly rates and the real return after inflation
Compare loans by total naira cost and plan debt repayment in a clear order
Check that insurers, pension administrators, fund managers and lenders are licensed by the right Nigerian regulator
Write and follow a Personal Financial Management Plan with a SMART goal and 90-day milestones
audience: Adult women who already handle household or business money and want a clear, structured way to measure, protect and grow their finances.
tools: A notebook and pen, or a phone with a notes or spreadsheet app
Access to your bank and wallet app statements
Internet access to check regulator websites (CBN, FCCPC, NAICOM, PenCom, SEC)

modules.title: Know Your Financial Position
modules.overview: Before you can manage money well, you need an honest picture of where you stand. In this module you build two simple personal financial statements, a net worth sheet and a monthly cash flow statement, and then score your financial health with five numbers you can recheck every quarter.

lessons.title: Your personal balance sheet: assets, debts and net worth
objectives: List everything you own that has money value and everything you owe
Calculate your net worth with one subtraction
Tell the difference between an asset that earns, one that holds value and one that loses value
Explain why net worth matters more than income alone

blocks.text: Most money advice starts with income: how much comes in each month. Income matters, but it only tells you about the flow of money. It does not tell you what you have built. Two women can each earn about ₦150,000 a month. One owns a sewing machine, a plot of land and some savings, and owes nothing. The other owes a loan app and a cooperative, and owns very little. Their income is the same, but their **financial position** is very different. The tool that shows this position is called a **personal balance sheet**, or a net worth statement.

blocks.name: personal-finance
blocks.alt: A woman reviewing her personal finances on a large screen
blocks.caption: A balance sheet is a snapshot of everything you own and owe on one day.

blocks.text: Three words you need

items: **Asset**: anything you own that has money value. Cash, money in a bank or wallet app, savings in a cooperative, land, a shop's stock, equipment such as a freezer or sewing machine, livestock, gold jewellery.
**Liability**: any money you owe. A bank loan, a loan app balance, money borrowed from a relative, unpaid stock taken on credit from a supplier, rent you owe the landlord.
**Net worth**: what is left when you subtract everything you owe from everything you own. **Net worth = total assets minus total liabilities.**

blocks.text: Net worth can be positive or negative. A negative number does not mean you are a bad person. It simply means that today your debts are bigger than what you own. The value of the balance sheet is that it turns a vague worry into a clear number you can work on.
Valuing what you own honestly

The rule is simple: write the amount you could **realistically get if you sold it this month**, not what you paid. A freezer bought for ₦250,000 three years ago may only sell for about ₦120,000 today. Clothes, phones and furniture lose value quickly, so many planners leave everyday household items out completely and only list things that could genuinely be sold. For land, use what similar plots in the same area are selling for, and be cautious. For a cooperative, use your savings balance, not your expected payout.

head: Type of asset
Examples
What usually happens to its value
rows: Shop stock, a grinding machine, a rented-out room, an investment fund
Usually keeps value, though cash loses buying power when prices rise

blocks.text: This table matters for decisions. When you have spare money, moving it into earning or holding assets builds net worth. Spending it on using assets is sometimes necessary, but it lowers net worth over time.

blocks.title: Two sides of the balance sheet
blocks.caption: Net worth is the gap between the left column and the right column.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's net worth on 1 March
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells foodstuff in a market in Enugu. She sits down with a notebook to list what she owns and owes. All naira amounts are illustrative.
steps: Assets: cash at home ₦18,000; bank account ₦62,000; Opay wallet ₦9,500; cooperative savings ₦140,000; stock in her shop (at cost) ₦230,000; deep freezer (resale value) ₦110,000.
Liabilities: cooperative loan balance ₦180,000; money borrowed from her sister ₦50,000; supplier credit for rice ₦75,000.
blocks.result: Ngozi's net worth is ₦264,500. She also notices that more than half of her assets (₦370,000) are stock and cooperative savings that she cannot turn into cash quickly, which tells her she needs more easy-to-reach savings.

blocks.text: Why the trend matters more than the number

One balance sheet is a photograph. Several balance sheets, done on the same date every three months, become a film. If Ngozi's net worth goes from ₦264,500 in March to ₦310,000 in June, she knows her money habits are building wealth, even if some weeks felt tight. If it falls, she can look at which line moved: did a loan grow, or did stock run down without being replaced?

Repaying debt also raises net worth, even though your cash goes down. Paying ₦50,000 back to her sister lowers Ngozi's cash by ₦50,000 and lowers her liabilities by ₦50,000, so net worth stays the same on the day. But next month she no longer needs to repay that money, and that frees future income.

blocks.title: Keep it private and keep it updated
blocks.text: Write your balance sheet in a notebook you keep safe or in a locked note on your phone. Do not post it in groups or share account balances with people you do not fully trust. Pick a fixed date, such as the first day of January, April, July and October, to update it.

blocks.title: Business and household together?
blocks.text: If your business and household money are mixed, list them together for now, but mark business items with a B. In later lessons you will see why separating them gives you clearer numbers.

takeaways: Net worth equals everything you own minus everything you owe
Value assets at what they would sell for now, not what you paid
Earning and holding assets build wealth; using assets lose value
Recalculate on the same date every quarter and watch the trend

activity.title: Build your first balance sheet
steps: Draw two columns on a page: Own and Owe.
List every asset with a realistic resale value, including bank, wallet and cooperative balances.
List every debt with the amount still owed today, including money owed to family and suppliers.
Add each column and subtract Owe from Own to find your net worth.
Circle the assets you could turn into cash within one week.
activity.evidence: A dated balance sheet page (photo or note) showing totals and net worth

lessons.title: Your monthly cash flow statement and savings rate
objectives: Build a one-page cash flow statement from a month of real records
Group spending into fixed, variable and occasional costs
Calculate your monthly surplus or deficit and your savings rate
Use a three-month view to plan with irregular income

blocks.text: Your balance sheet shows where you stand. Your **cash flow statement** shows how you got there. It is a summary of all the money that came in and went out over one period, usually a calendar month. Companies prepare one every year in their accounts. You can prepare a simple version on one page from the records you keep in a notebook, a spreadsheet or the transaction history of your bank and wallet apps.

blocks.name: financial-data
blocks.alt: A person reading financial charts and figures
blocks.caption: A cash flow statement turns a month of small transactions into a few clear totals.

blocks.text: Where to find a month of real numbers

items: **Bank and wallet statements**: most Nigerian bank apps and wallets such as Opay, Moniepoint and PalmPay let you download or view a statement for a date range. Every transfer, airtime purchase and POS payment is already recorded.
**Your notebook**: cash spending is not in any app, so it must be written down the same day.
**Receipts and invoices**: school fees, rent receipts, electricity tokens and supplier invoices.
**Memory, last**: estimates from memory are usually too low, so use them only to fill gaps and mark them as estimates.

blocks.text: Transfers between your own accounts are not income or spending. If you move ₦20,000 from your bank to your wallet, leave it out, or you will count the same money twice.
The layout

head: Section
What goes in it
Example lines
rows: All income received in the month
Salary, sales profit drawn from the business, side jobs, money received from family
Rent saved monthly, school bus, loan repayment, data plan
Large but not monthly, shown as a monthly share
School fees, gas refill, festive costs, health costs
Positive means money left over; negative means a shortfall

blocks.text: Occasional costs are the line most people forget. If school fees for two children are about ₦180,000 per term and there are three terms a year, the yearly cost is ₦540,000. Divided by 12, that is ₦45,000 a month. Showing that ₦45,000 every month stops fees from feeling like a shock.
Savings rate: the most useful single number

Your **savings rate** is the share of your income that you keep. **Savings rate = (money saved or used to reduce debt) divided by money in, times 100.** A rate of 10% means you keep ₦10 of every ₦100. There is no single correct rate for everyone. What matters is that it is positive and that you can see whether it rises or falls.

If your statement shows a **deficit**, the gap was covered somehow: by borrowing, by spending savings or by taking money out of business stock. Write down which one it was. A deficit covered by a loan app is far more urgent than one covered by a small dip into savings, because the loan carries interest and must be repaid from next month's income.

blocks.title: Worked example: Aisha's February cash flow
blocks.context: For example, Aisha is a nurse in Kano who also sells perfume oils on WhatsApp. She builds her February statement from her bank app, her Moniepoint wallet and her notebook. Amounts are illustrative.
steps: Money in: salary ₦185,000 + perfume profit ₦42,000 = ₦227,000.
Fixed costs: rent share ₦40,000 + data ₦6,000 + cooperative loan repayment ₦25,000 = ₦71,000.
Variable costs: food ₦68,000 + transport ₦22,000 + electricity ₦12,000 + other ₦15,000 = ₦117,000.
Occasional costs as a monthly share: school fees ₦20,000 + gas ₦4,000 = ₦24,000.
Savings rate: she saved the ₦15,000 surplus and also repaid ₦25,000 of loan principal, so (15,000 + 25,000) ÷ 227,000 × 100 = about 17.6%.
blocks.result: Aisha has a surplus of ₦15,000 and an effective savings rate of about 17.6%. She sees that food is her largest variable cost and decides to test buying grains in bulk once a month.

blocks.text: Irregular income: use a three-month view

If your income changes a lot, one month can mislead you. Put three months side by side. Use the **lowest** month's income as your planning figure for fixed costs, and treat anything above it as money to save or to put toward occasional costs. For example, if a hairdresser earned ₦140,000, ₦95,000 and ₦160,000 in three months, she plans her fixed costs around ₦95,000, not around the average of about ₦131,667.

blocks.title: From records to savings rate
blocks.caption: Follow the same five steps every month so the numbers can be compared.

blocks.title: Protect your statements
blocks.text: Bank statements show your account number, balances and who pays you. Never send them to strangers or to anyone who contacts you claiming to help with a loan. Download them yourself inside your own app.

takeaways: A cash flow statement summarises one month of money in and money out
Show occasional costs as a monthly share so they never surprise you
Savings rate is money kept divided by money in
With irregular income, plan fixed costs around your lowest month

activity.title: Prepare one month's cash flow statement
steps: Download or open last month's statements for every bank and wallet account you use.
Add cash spending from your notebook, and mark any figures that are estimates.
Remove transfers between your own accounts.
Fill in the five sections from the table and calculate the surplus or deficit.
Calculate your savings rate and write it at the top of the page.
activity.evidence: A one-page cash flow statement with the savings rate written on it

lessons.title: A financial health check with five numbers
objectives: Calculate five indicators of financial health from your two statements
Interpret each indicator and spot your weakest area
Choose one priority to work on first
Set a date to repeat the check

blocks.text: A doctor does not judge your health from one test. She checks blood pressure, weight, temperature and more, then looks for the reading that needs attention first. Money works the same way. With the balance sheet from lesson one and the cash flow statement from lesson two, you already have everything you need to calculate five simple indicators.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A woman ticking items on a large checklist
blocks.caption: Five numbers, checked every quarter, tell you which part of your finances needs attention first.

blocks.text: The five numbers

head: Indicator
How to calculate it
What it tells you
rows: Money saved or used to cut debt ÷ money in × 100
Whether you are building or standing still
How many months you could survive a shock
How much of your income is already promised to lenders
How much of what you own is really funded by borrowing
This quarter's net worth minus last quarter's
Whether your overall position is improving

blocks.text: **Essential monthly costs** means only what you must pay to live and work: food, rent, transport, utilities, school costs and loan repayments. It leaves out treats and celebrations. **Easy-to-reach savings** means money you can get within a few days without a penalty: cash, bank or wallet savings, not land or shop stock.

The **debt to assets** ratio needs one more word of explanation. If you own ₦500,000 of assets and owe ₦200,000, then 40% of what you own was really paid for with borrowed money. The lower this share, the more of your assets truly belong to you, and the more room you have if you ever need to borrow for a good reason.
Reading the results

Many financial educators suggest aiming, over time, for emergency savings covering three to six months of essential costs, and for a debt repayment ratio low enough that one bad month does not force new borrowing. Treat these as direction, not as rules. A woman starting from zero emergency cover is doing well if she reaches two weeks, then one month.

items: If emergency cover is below one month, every shock becomes a new loan. Building a small buffer usually comes first.
If the debt repayment ratio is high, a large part of every month's income is gone before it arrives. Module 2 shows you how to reduce debt in an organised order.
If debt to assets is above 100%, you owe more than you own, so net worth is negative. Stop new borrowing except in a true emergency.
If the savings rate is negative, you are spending more than you earn, often by borrowing or running down stock. Go back to your cash flow statement and find the biggest variable cost.

blocks.title: Worked example: Halima's quarterly check
blocks.context: For example, Halima is a teacher in Abuja with a small poultry side business. Her numbers for the quarter are illustrative.
steps: Savings rate: she kept ₦12,000 and repaid ₦30,000 of loans from income of ₦210,000: 42,000 ÷ 210,000 × 100 = 20%.
Emergency cover: easy-to-reach savings ₦45,000; essential monthly costs ₦150,000: 45,000 ÷ 150,000 = 0.3 months, about nine days.
Debt repayment ratio: repayments ₦30,000 ÷ income ₦210,000 × 100 = about 14%.
Debt to assets: liabilities ₦160,000 ÷ assets ₦520,000 × 100 = about 31%.
Net worth trend: ₦360,000 now minus ₦335,000 last quarter = up ₦25,000.
blocks.result: Four indicators are moving in the right direction. Her weak point is emergency cover, about nine days. Her first priority is to raise easy-to-reach savings to one month of essential costs, ₦150,000, before taking any new loan for the poultry business.

blocks.title: Quarterly money health check
blocks.caption: Answer each question yes or no; the first no is usually your first priority.

blocks.text: Choosing your one priority

It is tempting to fix everything at once, but plans with five goals usually fail. Take the first indicator that gets a no in the checklist and make it your focus for the next three months. Write one sentence: "By 30 June I will raise my emergency cover from nine days to one month by saving ₦35,000 a month in a separate account." One clear sentence is easier to keep than a long list of intentions.

Repeat the check every quarter on the same date you update your balance sheet. Over a year you will have four readings of each indicator, and you will be able to see real progress, or catch a problem early.

blocks.title: A note on honesty
blocks.text: These numbers are only for you. If you round them to look better, you lose the main benefit, which is seeing clearly. Use real figures, mark estimates, and correct them next time.

takeaways: Your two statements give you five health indicators
Emergency cover is measured in months of essential costs
The debt repayment ratio shows how much income is already promised
Work on the first weak indicator only, for three months at a time

activity.title: Run your own five-number check
steps: Copy the five indicators from the table into your notebook.
Calculate each one using your balance sheet and cash flow statement.
Answer the five checklist questions with yes or no.
Write one priority sentence with a date and a monthly amount.
Put the next check date in your phone calendar.
activity.evidence: A dated page showing your five numbers and your one priority sentence

quiz.q: Ngozi owns assets worth ₦400,000 and owes ₦250,000. What is her net worth?
quiz.explain: Net worth is assets minus liabilities: 400,000 minus 250,000 = ₦150,000.

quiz.q: A freezer was bought for ₦250,000 and would sell for about ₦100,000 today. Which value goes on the balance sheet?
options: Nothing, equipment is never an asset
quiz.explain: Assets are valued at what you could realistically get for them now, not the original price.

quiz.q: Aisha moves ₦30,000 from her bank account to her wallet app. How should this appear on her cash flow statement?
options: It should be left out because it is a transfer between her own accounts
quiz.explain: Moving money between your own accounts is neither income nor spending. Counting it would double the figures.

quiz.q: School fees are ₦150,000 per term, three terms a year. What monthly share should go in the cash flow statement?
quiz.explain: Yearly cost is 150,000 × 3 = ₦450,000. Divided by 12 months, that is ₦37,500 a month.

quiz.q: Halima has ₦60,000 in easy-to-reach savings and essential monthly costs of ₦120,000. What is her emergency cover?
quiz.explain: Emergency cover is savings divided by essential monthly costs: 60,000 ÷ 120,000 = 0.5 months.

quiz.q: A hairdresser earned ₦140,000, ₦95,000 and ₦160,000 over three months. Which figure should she use to plan her fixed costs?
quiz.explain: With irregular income, planning fixed costs around the lowest month means she can still pay them in a slow month.

modules.title: Interest, Credit and Protection: The Tools of Money
modules.overview: This module gives you the arithmetic and the products behind good financial decisions. You learn how interest and inflation really work, how to read and reduce debt, how credit history follows you in Nigeria, and how insurance, pensions and regulated savings products protect what you build.

lessons.title: The arithmetic of money: interest, compounding and inflation
objectives: Calculate simple and compound interest on savings or a loan
Convert a monthly or daily rate into a yearly picture
Use the rule of 72 to estimate doubling time
Work out whether savings are beating rising prices

blocks.text: Every savings account, loan, investment and price increase is driven by the same few calculations. Banks and lenders do these calculations every day. When you can do them too, even roughly on your phone calculator, you can no longer be confused by attractive-sounding rates. This lesson covers four tools: simple interest, compound interest, rate conversion and real return.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person using a large calculator
blocks.caption: Your phone calculator is enough for every calculation in this lesson.

blocks.text: Simple interest

**Simple interest** is paid only on the original amount, called the **principal**. The formula is: **interest = principal × rate × time**. If you save ₦100,000 at 10% a year simple interest for 3 years, the interest is 100,000 × 0.10 × 3 = ₦30,000, and you end with ₦130,000.
Compound interest

**Compound interest** is interest on the principal **plus** the interest already earned. Each year the interest is added, and next year's interest is calculated on the bigger amount. Using the same ₦100,000 at 10% a year compounded yearly: after year 1 you have ₦110,000; after year 2, 110,000 × 1.10 = ₦121,000; after year 3, 121,000 × 1.10 = ₦133,100. Compounding earned an extra ₦3,100 compared with simple interest. Over 10 or 20 years the gap becomes very large. Compounding works against you in exactly the same way when unpaid loan interest is added to what you owe.
Monthly and daily rates hide the real cost

Many loans in Nigeria, especially from loan apps and some informal lenders, quote a rate per month or even per day. A small-looking number can be very expensive over a year. A rate of 4% a month is 48% a year even before compounding. If unpaid interest compounds monthly, it becomes about 60% a year, because 1.04 multiplied by itself 12 times is about 1.60. A rate of 1% a day for a 30-day loan is about 30% for that single month.
Always ask a lender: what is the total amount I will repay, in naira, and over how many weeks or months? Comparing total repayment is easier and safer than comparing rates.

The same conversion works in your favour on savings. When a product says interest is added monthly or daily, the yearly growth is slightly higher than the quoted yearly rate, because each small payment of interest starts earning too. When comparing two savings products, ask for the effective yearly rate, sometimes written as the annual percentage yield, so you compare like with like.
The rule of 72

To estimate how long money takes to double at a yearly compound rate, divide 72 by the rate. At 12% a year, 72 ÷ 12 = about 6 years. At 8%, about 9 years. The same rule shows how fast a debt doubles if you do not pay: a debt growing at 24% a year doubles in about 3 years.
Inflation and real return

**Inflation** is the general rise in prices over time. Nigeria's official inflation rate is published by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) every month. When prices rise faster than your savings grow, your money buys less, even though the naira figure went up. The return after accounting for inflation is called the **real return**.

blocks.title: Worked example: is Blessing's savings account keeping up?
blocks.context: For example, Blessing keeps ₦200,000 in a savings account paying 5% a year. Suppose prices rise by 20% over the same year. These rates are illustrative, so use the current figures from your bank and the NBS.
steps: Savings after one year: 200,000 × 1.05 = ₦210,000.
Goods that cost ₦200,000 at the start of the year now cost 200,000 × 1.20 = ₦240,000.
Buying power: 210,000 ÷ 240,000 = 0.875, so her money buys 87.5% of what it bought a year earlier.
Real return: 0.875 minus 1 = minus 12.5%.
blocks.result: Blessing's balance grew by ₦10,000, but in real terms she lost about 12.5% of her buying power. Short-term emergency money still belongs somewhere safe and easy to reach, but money for goals several years away needs a product that aims to grow faster than prices, which Lesson 3 introduces.

blocks.title: Checking any rate in four steps
blocks.caption: Run any savings offer or loan through these four steps before you agree to it.

blocks.title: Returns that are too good to be true
blocks.text: If someone promises 20% or 30% a month with no risk, the arithmetic of the rule of 72 says the money would double every few months. No legitimate business can do that for long. Promises like this are a classic sign of a Ponzi scheme. Check whether the operator is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) before giving money.

takeaways: Simple interest is on the principal only; compound interest grows on itself
Turn monthly or daily rates into a yearly picture and a total naira cost
Divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate doubling time
Real return is growth after rising prices are taken into account

activity.title: Run the numbers on your own money
steps: Find the interest rate on one savings account or product you use and note whether it is per year or per month.
Calculate what ₦100,000 would become after one year in it.
Look up the latest headline inflation rate on the NBS website or in a trusted news report.
Calculate the real return using the method in the worked example.
Write one sentence on whether this product suits short-term or long-term money.
activity.evidence: A note showing the rate, the one-year balance, the inflation figure used and the real return

lessons.title: Using credit wisely: loan costs, credit history and a debt payoff plan
objectives: Compare flat-rate and reducing-balance loans by total cost
Explain how credit bureaus record your borrowing in Nigeria
List your debts and choose an avalanche or snowball payoff order
Check that a digital lender is approved before borrowing

blocks.text: Credit is not good or bad on its own. A loan that buys stock you can sell at a profit within weeks can build your business. A loan that pays for a party, then forces you to borrow again to repay it, can trap a household for years. This lesson gives you three skills: reading the true cost of a loan, protecting your credit history, and getting out of debt in an organised way.

blocks.name: credit-card-payments
blocks.alt: A person making a card payment
blocks.caption: Every repayment you make, or miss, can follow you into your credit history.

blocks.text: Flat rate or reducing balance?

Lenders calculate interest in two common ways. With a **flat rate**, interest is charged on the full original amount for the whole loan, even though you are paying it down. With a **reducing balance**, interest is charged only on what you still owe, so it gets smaller each month. Two loans with the same quoted rate can cost very different amounts.

blocks.title: Worked example: two offers for ₦200,000 over 6 months
blocks.context: For example, Funmi needs ₦200,000 for stock. Lender A charges 5% per month flat. Lender B charges 5% per month on a reducing balance with equal monthly payments. These are illustrative offers.
steps: Lender A interest: 200,000 × 0.05 × 6 = ₦60,000. Total repaid ₦260,000, or about ₦43,333 a month.
Lender B monthly payment (from a standard loan calculator): about ₦39,403. Total repaid about ₦236,421.
Lender B first month: interest 200,000 × 0.05 = ₦10,000, so about ₦29,403 reduces the debt. By month six, interest is only about ₦1,876.
Difference: 260,000 minus 236,421 = about ₦23,579 more with the flat rate.
blocks.result: Both lenders said 5% a month, but the flat-rate loan costs about ₦23,579 more. Funmi asks every lender for the total repayment in naira and a repayment schedule before she signs.

blocks.text: Your credit history in Nigeria

When you borrow from a bank, microfinance bank or many licensed lenders, your loan and how you repay it can be reported to credit bureaus licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). The licensed private bureaus include CRC Credit Bureau, FirstCentral Credit Bureau and CreditRegistry. Your records are linked to identifiers such as your BVN. A future lender can check this history, and late or unpaid loans can lead to refusal or higher rates.

items: You can request your own credit report from a bureau. Check each bureau's website for how to apply and any fee.
Check that every loan listed is really yours and that repaid loans show as closed. Ask the bureau and the lender to correct mistakes in writing.
Paying on time, every time, is the main way to build a good record.

blocks.text: Making a debt payoff plan

If you have several debts, list them all in one table with the amount owed, the interest rate and the minimum payment. Always pay the minimum on every debt. Then put any extra money on one debt at a time, using one of two well-known methods.

blocks.title: Two ways to order debt repayment
blocks.caption: Both work if you keep paying minimums on all debts and add extra to one at a time.

blocks.text: With the avalanche method, extra money goes to the loan app first, because it costs ₦4,800 a month. With the snowball method, extra money goes to the sister first, because clearing a whole debt quickly can give motivation. If a debt carries a very high rate, like the loan app here, the avalanche order usually saves the most. Whichever you choose, once a debt is cleared, add its payment to the next one.

If you can see that you will miss a payment, contact the lender **before** the due date. Explain what happened, propose an amount you can truly pay and ask for any new arrangement in writing. Many banks, microfinance banks and cooperatives prefer a restructured plan to a default. Do not take a new loan to repay an old one unless it is clearly cheaper and you have a plan to stop borrowing.

blocks.title: Digital loans: check before you borrow
blocks.text: The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) regulates digital and online lenders and publishes a list of approved lenders on its website. Before installing a loan app, check that it is on the list. Do not give an app access to your contacts or photos, never pay an upfront fee to receive a loan, and report harassment or threats to the FCCPC.

blocks.title: A simple borrowing test
blocks.text: Before any loan, write down: what the money is for, how it will produce the repayment, the total naira cost and what you will do if repayment is late. If you cannot answer the second question, the loan is likely to add pressure, not reduce it.

takeaways: Compare loans by total naira repaid, not by the quoted rate
Flat-rate interest costs more than reducing-balance at the same rate
Your repayment record is shared with CBN-licensed credit bureaus
Pay all minimums, then target one debt at a time

activity.title: Build your debt table and payoff order
steps: List every debt with balance, interest rate (or fee) and minimum payment.
Calculate this month's interest cost for each debt.
Choose avalanche or snowball and number your debts in payoff order.
Decide on an extra monthly amount and write which debt receives it.
If you use any loan app, check it against the FCCPC approved list.
activity.evidence: A debt table with payoff order and the extra monthly amount written on it

lessons.title: Protecting what you build: insurance, pensions and regulated long-term savings
objectives: Describe how insurance, pensions and long-term savings protect a household
Name the regulator to check for each type of financial product in Nigeria
Explain how the Micro Pension Plan serves self-employed women
Order your financial priorities using the security pyramid

blocks.text: Budgeting and saving build money. Protection stops one event from wiping it out. A hospital stay, a fire in a shop or a husband's sudden death can take years of savings in a week. In Nigeria many people rely on family and community support in such moments, and that support is valuable, but it is not always enough or available. Three formal tools help: insurance, pensions and regulated long-term savings.

blocks.name: closed-umbrella
blocks.caption: Insurance is like an umbrella: you pay for it in good weather so it is ready for the storm.

blocks.text: Insurance: sharing risk

Insurance works by pooling. Many people each pay a small, regular amount called a **premium**. When one of them suffers a covered loss, the insurer pays a claim from the pool. Insurance companies in Nigeria are licensed and supervised by the **National Insurance Commission (NAICOM)**. Some useful types for women and small businesses are:

items: **Health insurance**: the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) oversees health insurance nationally, and many states run their own health insurance agencies with plans for informal workers. Ask your state agency or a nearby primary health centre what plans are available.
**Micro-insurance**: low-premium cover sold through banks, cooperatives or mobile platforms, for example cover for shop stock, hospital cash or funeral costs.
**Life insurance**: pays your named beneficiaries if you die during the cover period, so children's school costs can continue.

blocks.text: Before you buy, read what is **excluded**, how to make a claim, how long payment takes and whether the insurer appears on NAICOM's list of licensed operators.

Once you have a policy, keep the policy document, premium receipts and the insurer's claims contact together with your other important papers. Tell your beneficiaries that the policy exists and where the papers are. If something happens, report it to the insurer as soon as possible, take photos of any damage and keep copies of everything you send. A claim is much easier when the paperwork is ready.
Pensions: income for later life

Nigeria's Contributory Pension Scheme is regulated by the **National Pension Commission (PenCom)**. Each person has a **Retirement Savings Account (RSA)** managed by a licensed Pension Fund Administrator (PFA). For employees covered by the Pension Reform Act 2014, the minimum contribution is 10% of monthly pay from the employer and 8% from the employee. If you are employed, check your RSA statement through your PFA's app or website to confirm contributions are arriving.

Most women in trading, farming and services are self-employed, so no employer contributes. PenCom's **Micro Pension Plan** lets self-employed and informal sector workers open an RSA and contribute amounts that suit them, as often as they choose. Under the plan, part of the contributions can be accessed for emergencies, according to the rules your PFA explains. Name your beneficiaries when you open the account and update them if your family changes.
Regulated long-term savings

head: Product
Who issues or manages it
Who regulates or backs it
rows: CBN; deposits insured by NDIC up to a limit
Debt Management Office (DMO), sold via stockbrokers
Issued for the Federal Government, bought through banks
Money market and other mutual funds

blocks.text: These products carry different levels of risk and return. Government securities and bank deposits are generally lower risk. Mutual funds can go up and down. None of them should promise a fixed, very high monthly return. Check current rates and minimum amounts on the official websites, as they change.

blocks.title: Worked example: what small regular contributions can become
blocks.context: For example, Comfort is a 38-year-old tailor in Port Harcourt who opens a Micro Pension account. She pays ₦60,000 at the start of each year (₦5,000 a month). Assume an illustrative return of 10% a year; real returns vary and are not guaranteed.
steps: She paid in 60,000 × 3 = ₦180,000, so growth added ₦38,460.
blocks.result: After three years Comfort's ₦180,000 has become about ₦218,460 at the assumed rate. Because growth compounds, the longer she continues, the larger the share of her balance that comes from returns rather than from her own payments.

blocks.title: The financial security pyramid
blocks.caption: Build from the bottom: emergency savings first, long-term investments last.

blocks.title: Verify the licence every time
blocks.text: Before giving money to any insurer, fund manager, investment platform or pension agent, search its name on the website of the matching regulator: NAICOM, SEC, PenCom or CBN. Pay only into an account in the company's registered name, never into a personal account.

takeaways: Insurance shares risk so one event does not wipe out savings
NAICOM licenses insurers, PenCom pensions, SEC fund managers, CBN banks
The Micro Pension Plan lets self-employed women build retirement savings
Build protection from the bottom of the pyramid upwards

activity.title: Map your protection gaps
steps: Draw the five-level pyramid and tick each level you already have in place.
For the lowest unticked level, write one product that could fill it.
Find the matching regulator's website and confirm the provider is licensed.
Write down the premium or contribution you could afford each month.
Note who your beneficiaries or next of kin would be.
activity.evidence: Your ticked pyramid with one named, verified product and a monthly amount

quiz.q: ₦100,000 is saved at 10% a year compounded yearly. What is the balance after 2 years?
A loan app charges 4% per month. Roughly what is that as a yearly rate before compounding?
quiz.explain: 4% a month × 12 months = 48% a year, and more if unpaid interest compounds.

quiz.q: Two lenders both quote 5% per month on ₦200,000 for 6 months. One is flat rate, one is reducing balance. Which costs less in total?
options: It depends only on the lender's name
quiz.explain: Reducing-balance interest is charged only on what is still owed, so total interest is lower than a flat rate on the full original amount.

quiz.q: Kemi has three debts and extra money each month. She wants to pay the least total interest. Which debt should get the extra money first?
options: The one with the smallest balance
The one with the highest interest rate
quiz.explain: The avalanche method targets the highest interest rate first, which saves the most interest overall.

quiz.q: Ada wants to check whether an insurance company is licensed in Nigeria. Where should she look?
quiz.explain: The National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) licenses and supervises insurers.

quiz.q: A self-employed market trader with no employer wants to save for retirement in a regulated account. Which option fits best?
options: A WhatsApp investment group promising 25% a month
PenCom's Micro Pension Plan through a licensed PFA
quiz.explain: The Micro Pension Plan is designed for self-employed and informal workers and is regulated by PenCom.

modules.title: Financial Independence, Good Partnerships and Your Plan
modules.overview: The final module turns knowledge into protection and action. You secure your own financial identity and records, learn to deal confidently with banks, cooperatives and other providers, and assemble everything into a Personal Financial Management Plan with a clear 90-day path.

lessons.title: Financial independence: your own accounts, records and next of kin
objectives: Set up the basic financial identity every adult woman needs
Create a household asset and document register
Recognise signs of financial control in a relationship and plan safe responses
Name next of kin and beneficiaries on your accounts

blocks.text: Many women contribute to household money, through salaries, trading, farming or unpaid work that saves the family money, but have little control over it or little record of it. When a marriage ends, a husband dies or a family dispute starts, a woman without her own account, her own records and her name on property can lose what she helped build. Financial independence does not mean keeping secrets from your partner. It means you can act, prove and protect your share if you ever need to.

blocks.name: personal-documents
blocks.alt: A woman organising personal documents in folders
blocks.caption: Your own documents and records are the foundation of financial independence.

blocks.text: Your financial identity

items: **National Identification Number (NIN)** from NIMC, needed for bank accounts, SIM registration and many government services.
**Bank Verification Number (BVN)**, linked to every bank account you open. One BVN covers all your banks.
**At least one account in your own name only**, at a licensed bank or microfinance bank, with your own phone number linked to it and your own PIN that you never share.
**Your own email address and phone number** for alerts, so messages about your money come to you.

blocks.text: If your business is registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), keep a copy of the certificate and open the business account in the business name. Keeping business money separate from household money makes your records clearer and makes it easier to show what the business has earned.
The household asset and document register

A register is a simple list of every important asset and where the proof is kept. It should include land and property documents, vehicle papers, bank and pension accounts, insurance policies, cooperative passbooks and any money owed to you. Write who paid for each item, or what share you contributed. Keep originals in a safe place and copies, or phone photos, in a second safe place, such as a secured cloud folder or with a trusted relative.

blocks.title: Worked example: Amaka's register
blocks.context: For example, Amaka and her husband in Onitsha bought a plot and built a shop together. She has receipts in different bags and drawers. She spends one Saturday building a register. Amounts are illustrative.
steps: She lists five items: the plot (receipt and survey plan in her husband's name, she contributed ₦800,000 of ₦2,000,000), the shop building (she paid ₦350,000 for roofing, receipts kept), her savings account, her Micro Pension RSA and her cooperative passbook.
She calculates her share of the plot: 800,000 ÷ 2,000,000 × 100 = 40%.
She photographs each receipt and document and saves them in a password-protected folder on her phone.
She speaks with her husband calmly about adding her name to the plot documents, and they agree to visit a lawyer together.
She writes the date of the register and a reminder to update it every six months.
blocks.result: Amaka now has proof of a 40% contribution to the plot, the roofing receipts for the shop and a list of every account. If a dispute ever arises, she is not relying on memory.

blocks.title: Financial independence checklist
blocks.caption: Tick each item; any unticked item is your next step.

blocks.text: When money is used to control

Sometimes a partner or relative controls money in a harmful way: taking all of a woman's earnings, refusing her access to any money, forcing her to take loans in her name, or stopping her from working. This is often called **financial abuse**. It is not a normal family disagreement. If this is happening, safety comes first. Keep a small amount of money and copies of key documents where only you can reach them, and talk to someone you trust, such as a women's group leader, a religious leader you trust, a lawyer, or a legal aid or women's support organisation in your state.
Next of kin, beneficiaries and wills

Every bank account, pension RSA and insurance policy lets you name a next of kin or beneficiary. Check these regularly, because an out-of-date name can delay money reaching your children. A **will** is a written document saying who should receive your property after death. Rules on wills and inheritance differ by state and can also be affected by customary and religious law, so it is wise to speak with a lawyer to make a valid will.

blocks.title: Protect your PIN and BVN
blocks.text: No bank, regulator or genuine agent will ask for your PIN, password or OTP. Do not let anyone, including family members, operate your accounts with your PIN. If you think someone knows it, change it in your bank app or at a branch immediately.

blocks.title: Start the conversation early
blocks.text: Talking about whose name is on property is easier when the relationship is calm. Frame it as protecting the children and the family's future, not as distrust.

takeaways: Have NIN, BVN and at least one account in your own name
Record every asset, your contribution and where the proof is kept
Financial abuse is a safety issue; keep documents and seek trusted help
Name next of kin on every account and consider a valid will

activity.title: Start your asset and document register
steps: List every important asset and account in your household.
For each one, write whose name is on it, your contribution and where proof is kept.
Photograph each key document and store the photos in a secure folder.
Check the next of kin or beneficiary on two of your accounts and update if needed.
Tick the independence checklist and note your next step.
activity.evidence: A dated register page plus a note confirming next of kin checked on two accounts

lessons.title: Working with banks, cooperatives and advisers: ask, compare and complain
objectives: Ask the right questions before opening any financial product
Compare two savings offers by naira return and access
Check that a cooperative is properly run before joining
Escalate a complaint to the right regulator

blocks.text: A good relationship with financial providers is a partnership: you bring your money and loyalty, and they should bring clear terms, safety and good service. Many people accept whatever the staff member says because they feel rushed or unsure. With a short set of questions, you can take control of every conversation, whether you are at a bank branch, talking to a fintech agent or joining a cooperative.

blocks.name: online-banking
blocks.alt: A woman using online banking on her phone
blocks.caption: Whether in a branch or in an app, the same questions protect you.

blocks.text: Six questions before you sign

items: What is the total I will earn, or pay, in naira, and over what period?
What fees or charges apply, including account maintenance, transfer, card and early withdrawal charges?
How quickly can I get my money back, and is there a penalty for withdrawing early?
Who licenses or regulates this product, and can I see it on the regulator's website?
What happens if I miss a payment or the provider closes?
Can I have the terms in writing, or a link to them, before I agree?

blocks.text: If a staff member or agent cannot answer, or tells you not to worry about the details, take that as a reason to wait. A good product can be explained clearly.

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing two savings offers
blocks.context: For example, Grace has ₦300,000 she will not need for six months. Offer A is a bank fixed deposit at 12% a year for six months, with a penalty on early withdrawal. Offer B is a flexible savings wallet at 8% a year, withdraw any time. The rates are illustrative.
steps: Offer A interest for six months: 300,000 × 0.12 × 6 ÷ 12 = ₦18,000.
Offer B interest for six months: 300,000 × 0.08 × 6 ÷ 12 = ₦12,000.
Difference: 18,000 minus 12,000 = ₦6,000 in favour of Offer A.
She asks both providers whether tax or charges are deducted from interest, and checks that the wallet's provider is licensed by the CBN.
She keeps one month of emergency money in Offer B and places the rest in Offer A.
blocks.result: Grace earns more on money she will not touch, while keeping emergency money flexible. She chose based on naira amounts and access, not on which advert looked better.

blocks.text: Checking a cooperative

Cooperatives can be excellent for savings and fair loans, and many WODDI members belong to one. A well-run cooperative is registered with the state's cooperative department, holds regular general meetings, keeps written records of every member's savings and loans, and has its accounts audited. Ask to see the registration certificate and the last annual report. Make sure every payment you make is recorded in your passbook or app the same day, and that money goes into an account in the cooperative's name, not a person's account.
Getting advice you can trust

Advice comes from many places: bank staff, agents, friends, social media influencers and group leaders. Before acting on it, ask two questions. First, **does this person earn money if I say yes?** A bank officer with a sales target or an agent paid per sign-up may be honest, but their advice is not neutral. Second, **can they show me the product's terms and licence?** Good advisers welcome questions and give you time to think. Be most careful with advice that arrives through WhatsApp or Telegram groups, comes with pressure to act today, or is backed only by screenshots of other people's profits.

Partnership also means checking your side. Read your account statement every month, even if only for five minutes. Look for charges you do not recognise, transfers you did not make and interest that was promised but not paid. Small errors found early are easy to fix, and your monthly check gives you the proof you need if you must complain.
When things go wrong: how to complain

Start with the provider. Put your complaint in writing, by email or through the official app, with your account name, dates, amounts and screenshots. Ask for a reference number. If the problem is not solved within the time the provider promises, or you get no answer, take it to the regulator for that type of product.

head: Type of provider
Where to escalate
rows: Banks, microfinance banks, payment and wallet companies
Central Bank of Nigeria consumer protection channels
Digital lenders and general consumer issues
Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC)

blocks.title: The complaint path
blocks.caption: Each step builds a written record that makes the next step stronger.

blocks.title: Fake helpers
blocks.text: People sometimes pose as bank staff or recovery agents on social media and offer to solve complaints for a fee. Use only contact details from the official website or app, and never share your PIN, password or OTP with anyone handling a complaint.

takeaways: Ask six questions and get the terms in writing before you sign
Compare offers by naira earned or paid and by how fast you can access money
A good cooperative is registered, audited and keeps written records
Complain in writing first, then escalate to the right regulator

activity.title: Compare and question two products
steps: Pick two savings or loan products you could use.
Ask both providers the six questions and write down the answers.
Calculate the naira return or cost of each for the same amount and period.
Check each provider on its regulator's website.
Write which one you choose and why, in two sentences.
activity.evidence: A comparison note with answers to the six questions and your naira calculations

lessons.title: Your Personal Financial Management Plan and 90-day action steps
objectives: Assemble your statements and checks into one written plan
Write a SMART savings goal with a monthly and weekly amount
Break the next 90 days into milestones you can track
Set a review routine that keeps the plan alive

blocks.text: You now have the pieces: a balance sheet, a cash flow statement, five health numbers, a debt table, a protection pyramid and an asset register. A **Personal Financial Management Plan** puts them together in a few pages, so you can see the full picture and decide what comes next. It is also the capstone for this course.

blocks.name: personal-goals
blocks.alt: A woman standing beside a board of personal goals
blocks.caption: A written plan turns good intentions into dated actions.

blocks.text: What goes in the plan

items: **Page 1, where I stand**: your latest balance sheet and net worth, and your five health numbers.
**Page 2, how money moves**: a household budget built from at least one month of actual tracked income and spending, with planned and actual figures side by side.
**Page 3, my goal**: one savings goal with a target amount, a date and a record of progress.
**Page 4, protection**: your debt payoff order, your pyramid gaps and your register status.
**Page 5, my next 90 days**: three milestones with dates and the action for each.

blocks.text: The budget page: planned against actual

Your budget page is the working heart of the plan. It is built from your tracked month, not from guesses. Each line shows what you planned, what really happened and the difference. Below is a short illustrative extract.

You do not need every line to match. Look for the one or two lines with the biggest difference and ask why. Was food over because prices rose, because of visitors, or because shopping was not planned? The answer tells you whether to change the budget figure or change the habit. Next month's planned figures should reflect what you learned.
Writing a SMART goal

A **SMART** goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. "Save more money" is not SMART. "Save ₦150,000 for one month of essential costs by 31 August, by putting ₦25,000 into my separate savings account every month" is SMART. The amount comes from your health check, the date gives a deadline, and the monthly figure must fit inside your cash flow surplus.

blocks.title: Worked example: Funke's goal and 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Funke runs a small restaurant in Ibadan. Her health check showed emergency cover of two weeks and essential monthly costs of ₦180,000. Her cash flow surplus is about ₦40,000 a month. Amounts are illustrative.
steps: Goal: one month of essential costs, ₦180,000. She already has ₦90,000 in easy-to-reach savings, so she needs 180,000 minus 90,000 = ₦90,000 more.
Time: at ₦30,000 a month, 90,000 ÷ 30,000 = 3 months. That leaves ₦10,000 of her ₦40,000 surplus as a margin for slow weeks.
Weekly amount: ₦30,000 × 12 months ÷ 52 weeks = about ₦6,923 a week, so she saves ₦7,000 every Monday.
Milestones: day 30, savings at ₦120,000; day 60, ₦150,000; day 90, ₦180,000.
Review: every Sunday evening she records the week's saving in her notebook and updates the total.
blocks.result: Funke's goal is specific, matches her real surplus and is broken into weekly actions. If she falls behind in one week, she can see it straight away and adjust the next week.

blocks.title: Your first 90 days
blocks.caption: Check progress at each milestone and adjust the next 30 days if needed.

blocks.text: Keeping the plan alive

Plans fail when they are written once and put away. Build three habits. **Weekly**, record income and spending and make your savings transfer on the same day. **Monthly**, compare planned and actual figures and note the biggest difference. **Quarterly**, update your balance sheet and five health numbers, and set the next 90-day goal. Each quarter's review is also the moment to move up the security pyramid: once your emergency cover goal is reached, the next goal might be clearing the most expensive debt or starting a Micro Pension contribution.

If a hard month comes, such as illness, a slow season or a family emergency, change the plan instead of abandoning it. Lower the monthly saving to a smaller amount you can keep, and write down the reason. A small saving you keep is worth more than a large one you abandon.

blocks.title: Share the plan with one accountability partner
blocks.text: Choose one trusted person, perhaps someone from your WODDI group, and agree to tell each other each month whether you reached your milestone. Share progress, not account details.

blocks.title: Keep your evidence
blocks.text: For the capstone you need your tracked month, your goal and progress record, and your 90-day plan. Photos of notebook pages or a simple spreadsheet are both fine.

takeaways: Your plan combines statements, goal, protection and a 90-day path
A SMART goal has an amount, a date and a monthly figure that fits your surplus
Break goals into weekly actions and 30-day milestones
Review weekly, monthly and quarterly; adjust rather than abandon

activity.title: Write your plan's goal and 90-day page
steps: Choose your goal from the first weak indicator in your health check.
Write it as a SMART sentence with amount, date and monthly figure.
Check that the monthly figure is smaller than your average surplus.
Convert it into a weekly amount and choose your saving day.
Write three dated milestones for days 30, 60 and 90.
activity.evidence: Your written SMART goal and a 90-day page with three dated milestones

quiz.q: Which step best protects a married woman's contribution to a plot of land registered in her husband's name?
options: Keeping receipts of her payments, recording her share in a register and discussing adding her name
Posting the receipts on social media
quiz.explain: Written proof of her contribution, a register and a calm conversation about the title documents give her real protection.

quiz.q: Grace has ₦200,000 for six months. Offer A pays 12% a year; Offer B pays 9% a year. How much more interest does Offer A give over six months?
Ifeoma's bank wrongly debited her account and has not replied to her written complaint. Where should she escalate it?
options: The Central Bank of Nigeria consumer protection channels
A person on Facebook offering to recover the money for a fee
quiz.explain: Complaints about banks that are not resolved go to the CBN's consumer protection channels. Paid 'recovery agents' on social media are a common scam.

quiz.q: Which sign suggests a cooperative is well run?
options: Members pay into the chairperson's personal account
There are no written records but everyone trusts each other
It is registered, holds general meetings and has audited accounts
It promises to double savings in three months
quiz.explain: Registration, regular meetings, records and audits are signs of a properly run cooperative.

quiz.q: Funke needs ₦90,000 more and saves ₦30,000 a month. How many months will it take?
In a hard month Bimpe cannot make her planned ₦25,000 saving. What is the best response?
options: Borrow from a loan app to make the saving
Lower the saving to an amount she can keep, note why, and continue
quiz.explain: Adjusting rather than abandoning keeps the habit alive, and borrowing to save adds cost and risk.

finalQuiz.q: Bisi owns assets worth ₦720,000 and owes ₦300,000. What is her net worth?
finalQuiz.explain: Net worth = assets minus liabilities = 720,000 minus 300,000 = ₦420,000.

finalQuiz.q: Which item is an earning asset?
options: A new phone used for chatting
A grinding machine that is rented out to customers
finalQuiz.explain: An earning asset brings in new money, as a grinding machine used for paid work does.

finalQuiz.q: Ronke's income was ₦200,000. She saved ₦20,000 and repaid ₦10,000 of loan principal. What is her savings rate?
Monthly debt repayments of ₦45,000 on income of ₦180,000 give what debt repayment ratio?
finalQuiz.explain: 45,000 ÷ 180,000 × 100 = 25% of income is already promised to lenders.

finalQuiz.q: ₦50,000 is saved at 20% a year compounded yearly. What is the balance after 2 years?
Using the rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 9% a year?
A savings account pays 6% a year while prices rise 15%. What is happening to the saver's buying power?
finalQuiz.explain: When inflation is higher than the interest rate, the real return is negative, so the money buys less.

finalQuiz.q: A lender charges 6% per month flat on ₦100,000 for 5 months. What is the total interest?
finalQuiz.explain: Flat interest = 100,000 × 0.06 × 5 = ₦30,000, charged on the full amount for every month.

finalQuiz.q: Before installing a loan app, which check matters most?
options: Whether it appears on the FCCPC list of approved digital lenders
Whether a friend has used it
Whether it asks for access to contacts
finalQuiz.explain: The FCCPC publishes approved digital lenders. Asking for contact access is a warning sign, not a reassurance.

finalQuiz.q: Which regulator should Ngozi check before buying a life insurance policy?
finalQuiz.explain: Insurers are licensed and supervised by the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM).

finalQuiz.q: Which action best protects a woman's financial independence?
options: Sharing her PIN with her husband so he can help
Keeping an account in her own name with her own phone for alerts
Keeping all receipts in one bag at her mother's house
Never naming a next of kin
finalQuiz.explain: An account in her own name, with alerts on her own phone and a private PIN, gives her control and a record.

finalQuiz.q: Esther's essential costs are ₦160,000 a month and she has ₦40,000 saved. She can save ₦20,000 a month. How long until she has one month of cover?

capstone.title: Personal Financial Management Plan
capstone.brief: A five-page Personal Financial Management Plan built from your own real numbers: a balance sheet and health check, a household budget based on at least one month of actual tracked income and expenses, a SMART savings goal with a target, timeline and documented progress, a protection page, and a 90-day plan naming your next financial goal and concrete steps.
steps: Track every naira of income and spending for at least one full month using your notebook and app statements.
Prepare your balance sheet and cash flow statement, then calculate your five health numbers.
Build a household budget from the tracked month, with planned and actual columns.
Choose one savings goal from your weakest indicator and write it as a SMART goal; record each payment toward it.
Complete your debt payoff order, protection pyramid and asset register.
Write a 90-day plan with three dated milestones and the next goal you will move to after this one.
evidence: Photos or file of one month of tracked income and expenses
Balance sheet with net worth and five health numbers, dated
Household budget with planned and actual figures
SMART savings goal with target, date and a progress record of at least four entries
Debt table with payoff order and protection pyramid with gaps marked
90-day plan with three dated milestones and the next financial goal named
